back2basics.concept: International Court of Justice and Genocide
back2basics.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations that settles disputes between states according to international law. Genocide is a crime defined by intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. The ICJ can rule on state responsibility for genocide but relies on the UN Security Council for enforcement, which can be blocked by veto powers.

2026-11-24-am-db94562763.deck: On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya community. This verdict is crucial for understanding international law on genocide, human rights enforcement, and the geopolitical complexities affecting justice.

back2basics.concept: Systemically Important Banks and Capital Buffers
back2basics.text: Systemically Important Banks are those whose failure could threaten the stability of the financial system. To mitigate this risk, regulators require these banks to maintain additional capital buffers beyond the minimum regulatory capital. The Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital is a key measure of a bank's financial strength, representing its core equity capital against risk-weighted assets. These buffers help ensure banks can absorb losses during financial stress, protecting depositors and the economy.

2026-11-24-am-f198330227.deck: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced the 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks, maintaining State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank as D-SIBs with specific additional capital requirements. body.label: Definition
body.text: D-SIBs are banks whose failure could disrupt the domestic financial system due to their size, complexity, and interconnectedness.

body.label: RBI Framework
body.text: The RBI issued the Framework for D-SIBs in 2014 and updated it in 2023, requiring disclosure of D-SIBs and assigning them to buckets based on their Systemic Importance Scores.

sections.heading: What are Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs)?

body.label: Banks Listed
body.text: State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank continue as D-SIBs under the same bucketing structure as in 2025.

body.label: Capital Buffer Requirements
body.text: These banks must maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital buffer over the capital conservation buffer, varying by bucket: SBI at 0.80%, HDFC Bank at 0.40%, and ICICI Bank at 0.20% of Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs).

sections.heading: Which banks are identified as D-SIBs in 2026 and what are their capital requirements?

body.label: Systemic Risk Mitigation
body.text: Additional capital requirements for D-SIBs reduce the risk of their failure impacting the broader financial system.

body.label: Regulatory Transparency
body.text: The RBI's disclosure of D-SIBs and their capital buffers enhances market discipline and regulatory oversight.

body.label: Global Coordination
body.text: Foreign banks designated as Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) with Indian branches must maintain proportionate CET1 capital surcharges in India, aligning with global standards.

back2basics.text: Judicial review allows courts to examine the legality of decisions made by educational institutions, ensuring they comply with principles of natural justice and fairness. mains.demand: Explain how judicial intervention upholds student rights and institutional accountability using the Kerala High Court case as an example.
mains.question: Examine the role of judiciary in protecting students' rights and ensuring accountability in educational institutions, with reference to the Kerala High Court's decision on the Sanskrit University students' suspension.

body: The Kerala High Court quashed the suspension and inquiry report against students, protecting their right to education and fair treatment.
The Court ensured students' access to examinations and campus during inquiries, preventing arbitrary denial of academic rights.
Judicial directions included counting suspension period towards any punishment, ensuring fairness in disciplinary processes.
The case illustrates judiciary's role in balancing institutional authority with individual rights and procedural justice.
structure.conclusion: Judicial oversight is crucial for safeguarding student rights and promoting accountability in educational governance.
structure.intro: Judiciary acts as a guardian of rights and fairness in educational institutions.

mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because the Court directed that examinations should not be withheld pending a fresh inquiry.

body.label: Suspension quashed
body.text: The High Court quashed the suspension order against 16 students affiliated with the Student Federation of India at the Sanskrit University.

body.label: Inquiry report set aside
body.text: The Court set aside the Enquiry Committee report that had found the students guilty of misconduct.

body.label: Examinations ordered
body.text: The Court directed the University to conduct a separate semester examination for these students within six weeks.

body.label: Campus access restored
body.text: The students were permitted to enter the campus and attend regular classes.

sections.heading: What did the Kerala High Court decide regarding the suspended students?

body.label: Protection during inquiry
body.text: The Court clarified that students cannot be suspended pending a fresh inquiry if initiated.

body.label: Suspension period counted
body.text: The 84 days of suspension already served must be counted towards any punishment if the students are found guilty after a fresh inquiry.

body.label: Exams not to be withheld
body.text: A fresh inquiry cannot be used as a reason to withhold examinations from the students.

sections.heading: Why does this matter for students’ rights and university governance?

body.label: Allegations against students
body.text: The students were accused of staging a mock cremation of the vice-chancellor, manhandling her, and attempting to damage university property.

body.label: Students’ denial
body.text: The students fully denied the allegations made against them.

body.label: Supreme Court involvement
body.text: The dispute escalated to the Supreme Court, which referred the matter back to the Kerala High Court with instructions to hold a separate exam if the High Court ruled in favor of the students.
